sections.html:
Wrightsville is the seat of Johnson County, and the 1895 courthouse anchors an older downtown that appraises differently from the farmhouses outside town. Expect listings to be acreage, wooded tracts or a farmhouse past the pavement. Land area is 303.02 square miles, with 30.3 residents per square mile in 2020.

Adrian is a quirk worth knowing. Its boundary with Emanuel County zigzags through town, so neighbors on one street can owe tax to different counties. Match an Adrian-area parcel to its county before you phone a tax office.

Home values are low and buyers are mostly local, many of them retired. A house priced near the $94,900 median draws more calls than one priced like a Macon listing, and financing often comes down to small loans or cash.

The county lost 791 residents between the 2010 and 2020 counts, and the 2025 estimate wins back only part of that. Some 88.5% of people were in the same house a year earlier, so turnover is slow.

Owners who still have a mortgage report median costs of $1,193 a month. Owners with the house paid off report $440. With median rent at $647, a paid-off home costs less per month than a rental.

A tax surprise stands out against a $440 monthly budget, and a delinquent balance adds interest at a pace that is hard to absorb on a fixed income. Asking for a payoff early gives you a number to plan around before a buyer appears. The tax commissioner's site also accepts online payment, which helps owners who live elsewhere.

Two tax offices share the building at 2484 West Elm Street, Wrightsville, ZIP 31096.

  • Tax Commissioner, (478) 864-2565 ext. 1: sends bills, takes payments, supplies payoff numbers and renews tags. Counter hours are weekdays, 8 until 4:30, and the commissioner's website accepts online payment.
  • Tax Assessors, (478) 864-3325 ext. 2: set value, take returns and exemption forms, and receive appeals. Search parcels through the assessors' qPublic page.
  • Clerk of Superior Court, 2557 East Elm Street, (478) 864-3484: holds recorded deeds.
  • Probate Court, (478) 864-3316: opens an estate when the person named on the deed has died.

The commissioner's page on the county site carries one unusual notice. Owners whose timber was damaged and then cut after Hurricane Helene can seek relief with a form from the Georgia Forestry Commission, attaching the documents it lists and delivering the packet to the commissioner. Anyone selling woodland should ask whether a claim exists for the parcel.

Georgia's fallback deadline is December 20, but counties may substitute December 1, November 15 or installment billing. Call the commissioner at (478) 864-2565 ext. 1 to get the date that applies to your bill.

Interest waits until 60 days after the postmark, and penalties may follow on late balances. The bill is addressed to the owner, so a lender holding escrow may never see a copy. Heirs should update the mailing address in writing.

If you are unsure whether you have paid, phone the commissioner with the parcel number before you list. A clean receipt in hand makes a buyer's title search shorter and keeps a closing from stalling over a small old balance.

Spring closings raise a common question: does the bill shift to the buyer? It does not. The owner on January 1 carries that year's tax, and nothing is refunded for a mid-year move, so the purchase contract has to divide it.

A Johnson County notice shows two numbers: the fair market value set for January 1, and the 40% slice of it that is actually taxed. An owner who buys or improves a parcel files a return during the first quarter, through April 1. Value left off a required return draws a 10% surcharge plus interest.

A challenge begins with a letter to the assessing board, postmarked within 45 days after the notice went out. The letter has to pick a path: an equalization board, a hearing officer, an arbitrator or superior court. The assessors can supply the state form.

Tax paid by mistake can be reclaimed through a written request filed inside three years. A refund that follows a won appeal is issued automatically.

Johnson County has no local homestead exemption, so the state's own exemptions are the only choice.

  • You qualify by owning the house and living in it as your legal residence, with the assessors deciding.
  • A form arriving after April 1 waits for the following year.
  • Once approved, the exemption continues until you move, sell or switch types.
  • Business personal property is returned every April 1, changed or not.
  • Mobile homes need a location permit within 30 days of being set, then a yearly renewal from January 1 through April 1.

To apply, take proof that you own the house and live in it to the Tax Assessors office at 2484 West Elm Street, and bring a copy of the deed if you recently bought. If you plan to sell soon, filing before April 1 still matters, because it lowers the bill that the January 1 owner carries for the whole year.

Business inventory can qualify for a freeport exemption where voters approved one. Request it at the assessors' desk during the return window.

Ask the commissioner for a written payoff figure, then have the Clerk of Superior Court's records searched for any lien on the parcel. Parcels that stay delinquent can reach the sales listed on the commissioner's tax sales page.

At the table, the closing agent pays the commissioner from what the seller would otherwise receive, and the lien clears as the deed records. A house passing through an estate has to go through Probate Court first. A buyer paying cash and taking the home as-is can absorb repairs, but the payoff, the recorded deed and any estate paperwork still happen.

If the seller has died, the Probate Court at (478) 864-3316 is the first call, since the person named on the deed cannot sign. Allow time for that step before you set a closing date.

A short checklist helps. Get the payoff in writing, confirm no lien is recorded, settle any estate filing, and tell the assessors about the change of owner so the next bill goes to the right person.

faqs.q: Who sends the Johnson County tax bill?
faqs.a: The commissioner's office at 2484 West Elm Street in Wrightsville mails it, and (478) 864-2565 ext. 1 reaches that desk. One bill carries the county, school and state levies. A question about the value itself goes to the assessors at (478) 864-3325 ext. 2.

faqs.q: Does Johnson County add a local homestead exemption?
faqs.a: No. Only the statewide exemptions are available, and the form has to reach the county by April 1 of the first year.

faqs.q: What is the Johnson County appeal window?
faqs.a: Owners get 45 days, counted from the day the notice went in the mail. The challenge is a letter to the assessing board naming the path you want.

faqs.q: What is a typical home worth in Johnson County?
faqs.a: About $94,900 at the median, based on 2020-2024 Census estimates for homes their owners live in. Renters pay a median of $647 monthly.

faqs.q: Does a January closing move the year's tax to the buyer?
faqs.a: Only if the contract says so. Whoever held title on January 1 owes the year, and the closing statement is where the parties divide it.
